title: Binary heap and priority queue explained: sift up, sift down and Python heapq — cv.cm
description: How a binary heap works: the heap property, array layout, sift up and sift down, heapify in O(n), priority queues and Python heapq, with code and complexity.
h1: Binary heap explained: priority queues, code and complexity
answer: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is smaller than or equal to its children (a min-heap) or larger than or equal to them (a max-heap). The smallest item is always at index 0, so you can read it in O(1), and insert or remove it in O(log n). Heaps are the standard way to implement a priority queue; in Python, use the `heapq` module.

body: Many programs repeatedly need the most urgent item from a changing collection: the next event in a simulation, the closest unvisited node in Dijkstra's algorithm, the task with the highest priority, or the k largest values in a stream. Sorting the whole collection after every insert costs O(n log n) each time. A sorted list makes removal cheap but insertion O(n). A heap makes both insert and remove-min O(log n), which is exactly what a priority queue needs.

body.note: A heap is only partially ordered. The minimum is at the top, but the rest of the array is not sorted. Do not expect `heap[1]` to be the second-smallest item.

sections.h: The idea: a tree stored in an array
body: A heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. That shape lets us store the tree in a plain list with no pointers.

Two repair operations keep the heap property. Sift up: after appending a new item at the end, swap it with its parent while it is smaller. Sift down: after moving the last item to the root, swap it with its smaller child while it is larger than that child. Each operation moves along one root-to-leaf path, so it does at most about log2(n) swaps.
Start with the min-heap `[2, 5, 3, 9, 6]` (2 is the root, its children are 5 and 3, and 5 has children 9 and 6).

ol: Push 1: append it, giving `[2, 5, 3, 9, 6, 1]`. Index 5 has parent index 2 (value 3).
1 is smaller than 3, swap: `[2, 5, 1, 9, 6, 3]`. Now index 2 has parent index 0 (value 2).
1 is smaller than 2, swap: `[1, 5, 2, 9, 6, 3]`. It reached the root, stop.
Pop: remove the root 1, move the last item 3 to the root: `[3, 5, 2, 9, 6]`.
Children of the root are 5 and 2; the smaller is 2, and 3 is larger, swap: `[2, 5, 3, 9, 6]`. Index 2 has no children, stop. The pop returned 1.

body: This class shows the mechanics. In real code use `heapq`, shown in the next section.

body.code:
class MinHeap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = []
    def push(self, x):
        a = self.a
        a.append(x)
        i = len(a) - 1
        while i > 0 and a[i] < a[(i - 1) // 2]:      # sift up
            p = (i - 1) // 2
            a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]
            i = p
    def pop(self):
        a = self.a
        top, last = a[0], a.pop()                   # IndexError if empty
        if a:
            a[0], i = last, 0
            while True:                             # sift down
                c = 2 * i + 1
                if c + 1 < len(a) and a[c + 1] < a[c]:
                    c += 1                          # pick the smaller child
                if c >= len(a) or a[i] <= a[c]:
                    break
                a[i], a[c] = a[c], a[i]
                i = c
        return top
h = MinHeap()
for x in [5, 3, 9, 1, 6, 2]:
    h.push(x)
print([h.pop() for _ in range(6)])  # [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9]

body: The `heapq` module works on an ordinary list and always keeps it a min-heap. `heapify` turns an existing list into a heap in place in O(n). To use priorities, push tuples: Python compares tuples element by element, so the first element is the priority. Add a counter as a tie-breaker so that items with equal priority never need to be compared directly.

body.code:
import heapq
from itertools import count
nums = [7, 2, 9, 4, 1]
heapq.heapify(nums)
print(nums[0], heapq.heappop(nums))      # 1 1
print(heapq.nlargest(2, [7, 2, 9, 4]))   # [9, 7]
tasks, order = [], count()
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, next(order), "write report"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, next(order), "fix outage"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, next(order), "reply to email"))
while tasks:
    priority, _, name = heapq.heappop(tasks)
    print(priority, name)
# 1 fix outage
# 2 write report
# 2 reply to email

body: For a max-heap, Python 3.14 added `heapq.heapify_max`, `heapq.heappush_max` and `heapq.heappop_max`. On older versions, the usual trick is to push negated keys, for example `heapq.heappush(h, -score)`, and negate again when you pop.

Time
Reason
rows: most nodes are near the bottom and move only a little

body: Building a heap by calling push n times costs O(n log n). `heapify` sifts down from the last parent to the root and costs O(n), so prefer it when you already have all the items.

ul: Max-heap: the same code with the comparison reversed; in Python, use the `_max` functions (3.14 and later) or negate the keys.
d-ary heap: each node has d children. A shallower tree makes push cheaper and pop slightly more expensive.

Indexed priority queue / decrease-key: `heapq` cannot change the priority of an item in place. A common workaround (used in Dijkstra's algorithm) is to push a new entry and skip outdated entries when they are popped.
Comparing incomparable items: pushing `(priority, dict)` raises `TypeError` when two priorities are equal, because Python then compares the dicts. Add a counter as the second tuple element.
Treating the heap list as sorted. Only `heap[0]` is guaranteed; use `sorted(heap)` if you need everything in order.
Off-by-one errors when mixing 1-based formulas (children `2i` and `2i + 1`) from textbooks with 0-based Python lists.

sections.h: When to use a heap and typical problems
body: Use a heap when you repeatedly need only the smallest or largest item from a collection that keeps changing. Use a sorted list or balanced tree when you also need ordered iteration or arbitrary deletions, and a plain `min()` when you only need the minimum once.

Classic uses: Dijkstra's shortest path and Prim's minimum spanning tree, merging k sorted lists (`heapq.merge`), finding the k largest or smallest items (keep a heap of size k, O(n log k)), the running median (two heaps), task schedulers and event-driven simulations, and heapsort.

faq.q: What is the difference between a heap and a priority queue?
faq.a: A priority queue is an abstract data type: insert items and remove the one with the highest priority. A binary heap is the most common data structure used to implement it.

faq.q: Is Python heapq a min-heap or a max-heap?
faq.a: The main functions such as `heappush` and `heappop` maintain a min-heap, so `heappop` returns the smallest item. Python 3.14 added separate `_max` functions for max-heaps; on older versions, store negated numbers.

faq.q: Why is heapify O(n) and not O(n log n)?
faq.a: Heapify sifts down each parent starting from the bottom. About half the nodes are leaves and do not move, a quarter move at most one level, and so on; the total work sums to O(n).

faq.q: Is a binary heap the same as a binary search tree?
faq.a: No. A BST orders left and right subtrees so you can search any key in O(log n). A heap only guarantees that each parent is smaller than its children, so it finds the minimum fast but searching for other keys is O(n).
No. Swaps during sift down can reorder equal keys. It sorts in place in O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space.
